```{r}
#| label: load-packages-r
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(nanoparquet)
library(glmnet)
library(rpart)
library(tidymodels)
library(scales)

# The factor zoo of lectures 10 to 13
sample_start <- ymd("1973-01-01")
sample_end <- ymd("2023-12-31")
test_start <- ymd("2000-01-01")
n_folds <- 5
ridge_lambdas <- 10^seq(-7, -1, by = 0.25)
lasso_lambdas <- 10^seq(-6, -2.5, by = 0.25)
macro_names <- c("dp", "tbl", "tms", "dfy", "svar")
test_years <- paste0(year(test_start), "–", year(sample_end))

# The rows of lectures 12 and 13 in the out-of-sample comparison: up to 60 PCA
# and RP-PCA factors, chosen by cross-validation; the tree and the forest of
# lecture 13
max_factors <- 60
phi_rp <- 10
tree_depth <- 2
min_leaf <- 500
n_trees <- 100
forest_grid <- expand_grid(mtry = c(1, 3, 7), min_n = c(500, 2000))

# The inputs and hidden units of the network for the forecasts. The slide
# "A feed-forward network" counts its parameters and draws the network; the
# code of the network defines the inputs again and uses the same 5 units
features <- c("ret_lag_1", "momentum_12", macro_names)
hidden_units <- 5
# Weights and constants: into the hidden layer, then into the output
n_parameters <- (length(features) + 1) * hidden_units + hidden_units + 1

months_per_year <- 12

# Colours of the slides, used by the figures
ku_red <- "#901A1E"
jet <- "#3d3d3d"
grey <- "#666666"
light <- "#e6e3df"
theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
)
```

```{python}
#| label: load-packages-py
#| include: false
from datetime import date

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
from sklearn.base import clone
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, PredefinedSplit
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor
```

```{r}
#| label: lectures-10-to-13-code
#| include: false
# The data, the ridge SDF and the forecast panel of lectures 10 to 13
osap_url <- paste0(
  "https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenSourceAP/CrossSection/resolve/",
  "Data-Release-2026.10/Portfolios/Full%20Sets%20OP/PredictorLSretWide.parquet"
)
osap_file <- "data/osap_long_short_returns.parquet"
if (!file.exists(osap_file)) {
  download.file(osap_url, osap_file, mode = "wb")
}
anomalies <- read_parquet(osap_file) |>
  mutate(date = floor_date(as.Date(date), "month")) |>
  filter(between(date, sample_start, sample_end)) |>
  select(date, where(\(x) !anyNA(x)))
returns <- as.matrix(select(anomalies, -date)) / 100
estimation <- anomalies$date < test_start
x_estimation <- returns[estimation, ]

sharpe_ratio <- function(x) mean(x) / sd(x) * sqrt(months_per_year)
ridge_weights <- function(x, lambda) {
  solve(crossprod(x) + nrow(x) * lambda * diag(ncol(x)), colSums(x))
}
folds <- ceiling(seq_len(nrow(x_estimation)) / (nrow(x_estimation) / n_folds))
cv_sharpe <- function(fit_weights, lambda) {
  map_dbl(seq_len(n_folds), \(k) {
    weights <- fit_weights(x_estimation[folds != k, ], lambda)
    sharpe_ratio(x_estimation[folds == k, ] %*% weights)
  }) |>
    mean(na.rm = TRUE)
}
ridge_lambda <- ridge_lambdas[which.max(map_dbl(ridge_lambdas, \(lambda) {
  cv_sharpe(ridge_weights, lambda)
}))]
ridge_sharpe <- c(
  estimation = sharpe_ratio(
    returns[estimation, ] %*% ridge_weights(x_estimation, ridge_lambda)
  ),
  test = sharpe_ratio(
    returns[!estimation, ] %*% ridge_weights(x_estimation, ridge_lambda)
  )
)

macro <- read_parquet("data/macro_predictors.parquet") |>
  transmute(date = date %m+% months(1), across(all_of(macro_names))) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(macro_names), \(x) {
    (x - mean(x[date < test_start])) / sd(x[date < test_start])
  }))
panel <- anomalies |>
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "anomaly", values_to = "ret") |>
  mutate(ret = ret / 100) |>
  arrange(anomaly, date) |>
  mutate(
    ret_lag_1 = lag(ret),
    momentum_12 = slider::slide_dbl(
      lag(ret),
      mean,
      .before = 11,
      .complete = TRUE
    ),
    .by = anomaly
  ) |>
  left_join(macro, join_by(date)) |>
  drop_na()
train <- panel |> filter(date < test_start)
test_rows <- panel$date >= test_start

covariance <- cov(x_estimation)
forecast_row <- function(method, forecast) {
  oos_r2 <- 1 -
    sum((panel$ret[test_rows] - forecast[test_rows])^2) /
      sum(panel$ret[test_rows]^2)
  portfolio <- panel |>
    mutate(forecast = forecast) |>
    select(date, anomaly, forecast, ret) |>
    nest(data = -date) |>
    mutate(
      ret = map_dbl(data, \(d) {
        order <- match(colnames(returns), d$anomaly)
        weights <- solve(
          covariance + ridge_lambda * diag(ncol(returns)),
          d$forecast[order]
        )
        sum(weights * d$ret[order])
      })
    )
  tibble(
    method = method,
    oos_r2 = oos_r2,
    estimation = sharpe_ratio(portfolio$ret[portfolio$date < test_start]),
    test = sharpe_ratio(portfolio$ret[portfolio$date >= test_start])
  )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: lectures-10-to-13-rows
#| include: false
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(lasso_lambdas, max_factors, phi_rp, tree_depth, min_leaf, n_trees, forest_grid, ridge_lambda, rlang::hash(panel), rlang::hash(returns))
# The other rows of the out-of-sample comparison, with the code of
# lectures 10 to 13
portfolio_sharpe <- function(weights) {
  c(
    estimation = sharpe_ratio(returns[estimation, ] %*% weights),
    test = sharpe_ratio(returns[!estimation, ] %*% weights)
  )
}
lasso_weights <- function(x, lambda) {
  fit <- glmnet(
    x,
    rep(1, nrow(x)),
    lambda = lambda,
    intercept = FALSE,
    standardize = FALSE,
    control = list(thresh = 1e-12)
  )
  as.vector(coef(fit))[-1]
}
components <- function(x) eigen(cov(x), symmetric = TRUE)$vectors
pc_lasso_weights <- function(x, lambda) {
  components(x) %*% lasso_weights(x %*% components(x), lambda)
}
factor_weights <- function(x, k, phi = 0) {
  mu <- colMeans(x)
  vectors <- eigen(cov(x) + phi * tcrossprod(mu), symmetric = TRUE)$vectors
  loadings <- vectors[, seq_len(k), drop = FALSE]
  factors <- x %*% loadings
  loadings %*% solve(cov(factors), colMeans(factors))
}
choose <- function(fit_weights, lambdas) {
  lambdas[which.max(map_dbl(lambdas, \(l) cv_sharpe(fit_weights, l)))]
}

market <- read_parquet("data/factors_ff3_monthly.parquet") |>
  filter(between(date, sample_start, sample_end))
lasso_lambda <- choose(lasso_weights, lasso_lambdas)
pc_lasso_lambda <- choose(pc_lasso_weights, lasso_lambdas)
pca_factors <- choose(\(x, k) factor_weights(x, k), seq_len(max_factors))
rp_pca_factors <- choose(
  \(x, k) factor_weights(x, k, phi_rp),
  seq_len(max_factors)
)
sdf_rows <- tibble(
  Portfolio = c(
    "Market",
    "1/N over all anomalies",
    "Plug-in mean-variance",
    "Ridge (prior on Sharpe ratios)",
    "Lasso on anomalies",
    "Lasso on principal components",
    "PCA",
    paste0("RP-PCA, φ = ", phi_rp)
  ),
  Inputs = c(
    "Market",
    rep(paste(ncol(returns), "anomalies"), 3),
    paste(sum(lasso_weights(x_estimation, lasso_lambda) != 0), "anomalies"),
    paste(
      sum(
        lasso_weights(
          x_estimation %*% components(x_estimation),
          pc_lasso_lambda
        ) !=
          0
      ),
      "components"
    ),
    paste(c(pca_factors, rp_pca_factors), "factors")
  ),
  sharpe = list(
    c(
      estimation = sharpe_ratio(market$mkt_excess[market$date < test_start]),
      test = sharpe_ratio(market$mkt_excess[market$date >= test_start])
    ),
    portfolio_sharpe(rep(1 / ncol(returns), ncol(returns))),
    portfolio_sharpe(ridge_weights(x_estimation, 0)),
    ridge_sharpe,
    portfolio_sharpe(lasso_weights(x_estimation, lasso_lambda)),
    portfolio_sharpe(pc_lasso_weights(x_estimation, pc_lasso_lambda)),
    portfolio_sharpe(factor_weights(x_estimation, pca_factors)),
    portfolio_sharpe(factor_weights(x_estimation, rp_pca_factors, phi_rp))
  )
) |>
  unnest_wider(sharpe)
# The best SDF with constant weights in the test sample
lasso_row <- filter(sdf_rows, Portfolio == "Lasso on anomalies")

# Lecture 13: the tree of depth 2 and the forest tuned on blocks of months
tree <- rpart(
  ret ~ momentum_12 + ret_lag_1,
  data = train,
  control = rpart.control(maxdepth = tree_depth, minbucket = min_leaf, cp = 0)
)
forest_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_formula(ret ~ ret_lag_1 + momentum_12 + dp + tbl + tms + dfy + svar) |>
  add_model(
    rand_forest(mtry = tune(), min_n = tune(), trees = n_trees) |>
      set_engine("ranger", seed = 2027) |>
      set_mode("regression")
  )
block_folds <- train |>
  mutate(block = ceiling(dense_rank(date) / (n_distinct(date) / n_folds))) |>
  group_vfold_cv(group = block, v = n_folds)
forest_tuning <- tune_grid(forest_workflow, block_folds, grid = forest_grid)
forest_fit <- forest_workflow |>
  finalize_workflow(select_best(forest_tuning, metric = "rmse")) |>
  fit(train)
tree_row <- forecast_row(
  paste("Tree of depth", tree_depth),
  predict(tree, panel)
)
forest_row <- forecast_row("Random forest", predict(forest_fit, panel)$.pred)
```

## From forests to networks

- **Lectures 10 to 12:** the SDF of the zoo with constant weights. Shrinkage of all anomalies leads the out-of-sample comparison: in `r test_years`, the lasso earns a Sharpe ratio of `r number(lasso_row$test, 0.01)`, the ridge SDF `r number(ridge_sharpe[["test"]], 0.01)`
- **Lecture 13:** forecasts of each anomaly's return from its last return, its momentum and `r length(macro_names)` macro predictors. The portfolio of the random forest's forecasts earns `r number(forest_row$test, 0.01)`
- Both uses of machine learning can take a more flexible function: a neural network

::: {.highlight}
**Today:** neural networks, first for the forecasts of lecture 13, then for the SDF itself (Chen, Pelger & Zhu, 2024): each anomaly's weight depends on the state of the economy, and a second network chooses the test assets. Can flexibility beat the linear SDFs?
:::

# Neural networks

## A feed-forward network

::: {.box}
Build a flexible function $g(z)$ from simple pieces: each **neuron** takes a weighted sum of its inputs and passes it through a nonlinear **activation function**
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$
h^{(1)} = \sigma\big(W^{(1)} z + c^{(1)}\big), \quad h^{(2)} = \sigma\big(W^{(2)} h^{(1)} + c^{(2)}\big), \quad g(z) = w' h^{(L)} + c
$$

- $\sigma(x) = \max(x, 0)$ (ReLU) or the logistic function. Without $\sigma$, the network would be linear regression
- With enough neurons, a network approximates any continuous function (Hornik, Stinchcombe & White, 1989). The price: many parameters, here `r n_parameters` already for one layer of `r hidden_units` neurons and `r length(features)` inputs

```{r}
#| label: plot-network
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 2.7
# The network of the forecasts: the inputs of lecture 13, one hidden layer
input_names <- c(
  "Last return",
  "Momentum",
  "Dividend-price ratio",
  "T-bill rate",
  "Term spread",
  "Default spread",
  "Stock variance"
)
n_inputs <- length(features)
# Nodes of a layer spaced as the inputs, centred on zero
spread <- function(n) seq(1, -1, length.out = n) * (n - 1) / (n_inputs - 1)
nodes <- tibble(
  layer = rep(1:3, c(n_inputs, hidden_units, 1)),
  y = c(spread(n_inputs), spread(hidden_units), 0)
)
edges <- bind_rows(
  expand_grid(from = which(nodes$layer == 1), to = which(nodes$layer == 2)),
  expand_grid(from = which(nodes$layer == 2), to = which(nodes$layer == 3))
) |>
  mutate(
    x = nodes$layer[from],
    y = nodes$y[from],
    xend = nodes$layer[to],
    yend = nodes$y[to]
  )
layer_titles <- c(
  "Inputs~italic(z)",
  "Hidden~layer~italic(h)^'(1)'",
  "Output~italic(g)(italic(z))"
)
parameter_counts <- c(
  str_glue("{n_inputs} × {hidden_units} weights + {hidden_units} constants"),
  str_glue("{hidden_units} weights + 1 constant")
)
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data = edges,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    color = "#b3b3b3",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = nodes,
    aes(x = layer, y = y, fill = factor(layer)),
    shape = 21,
    size = 7,
    color = "white",
    stroke = 1
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0.93,
    y = spread(n_inputs),
    label = input_names,
    hjust = 1,
    size = 4.2,
    color = jet
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 1:3,
    y = 1.35,
    label = layer_titles,
    parse = TRUE,
    size = 5,
    color = jet
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = c(1.5, 2.5),
    y = -1.3,
    label = parameter_counts,
    size = 4.2,
    color = grey
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(grey, ku_red, jet), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.2, 3.2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1.45, 1.5)) +
  theme_void()
```
:::

## Training a network

- **Loss:** the mean squared forecast error, as for OLS, but without a closed form. **Gradient descent** moves the vector $\theta$ of all weights and constants (every $W$, $c$ and $w$) a small step $\eta$ against the gradient of the loss, step $s$ after step:

$$
\theta^{(s+1)} = \theta^{(s)} - \eta\, \nabla_\theta \, \frac{1}{|B_s|} \sum_{(i,t) \in B_s} \big(r_{i,t+1} - g(z_{i,t}; \theta^{(s)})\big)^2
$$

- **Mini-batches:** $B_s$ holds all anomaly-months $(i, t)$ of the estimation sample, or, with many observations, a small random subset of them, new in every step. Each step is cheaper but noisier: **stochastic** gradient descent
- **Backpropagation:** the chain rule gives the gradient for all layers in one backward pass, from the output to the first layer

## Regularization

- **Weight decay:** a ridge penalty on the weights
- **Early stopping:** stop when the loss in a validation sample rises; the validation sample also chooses the penalty
- **Dropout:** switch off random neurons during training
- **Ensembles:** average networks from different random starts
- Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020) use all of them; their best networks have three or four layers

```{r}
#| label: network-data-r
#| include: false
# The predictors of lecture 13, standardized with the estimation sample, and
# the return in units of its standard deviation there, which gives the weight
# decay a scale
features <- c("ret_lag_1", "momentum_12", "dp", "tbl", "tms", "dfy", "svar")
ret_sd <- sd(train$ret)
scaled_panel <- panel |>
  mutate(
    across(all_of(features), \(x) {
      (x - mean(x[date < test_start])) / sd(x[date < test_start])
    }),
    ret_scaled = ret / ret_sd
  )
scaled_train <- filter(scaled_panel, date < test_start)
```

```{python}
#| label: network-data-py
#| include: false
#| eval: false
# The predictors of lecture 13, standardized with the estimation sample, and
# the return in units of its standard deviation there, which gives the weight
# decay a scale
features = ["ret_lag_1", "momentum_12", "dp", "tbl", "tms", "dfy", "svar"]
in_estimation = pl.col("date") < test_start
ret_sd = train["ret"].std()
scaled_panel = panel.with_columns(
    [
        (pl.col(c) - pl.col(c).filter(in_estimation).mean())
        / pl.col(c).filter(in_estimation).std()
        for c in features
    ],
    ret_scaled=pl.col("ret") / ret_sd,
)
scaled_train = scaled_panel.filter(in_estimation)
```

## Tuning the weight decay

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: tune-network-r
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(rlang::hash(scaled_train), features)
validation_start <- ymd("1995-01-01")
decay_grid <- tibble(penalty = c(1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000))

# Estimate until validation_start, choose the weight decay on the years after
validation_split <- make_splits(
  filter(scaled_train, date < validation_start),
  assessment = filter(scaled_train, date >= validation_start)
)
validation <- manual_rset(list(validation_split), ids = "validation")
network_model <- mlp(hidden_units = 5, penalty = tune(), epochs = 500) |>
  set_engine("nnet") |>
  set_mode("regression")
network_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_variables(outcomes = ret_scaled, predictors = all_of(features)) |>
  add_model(network_model)
set.seed(1) # tune_grid() draws the random starts of the networks
network_tuning <- tune_grid(network_workflow, validation, grid = decay_grid)
best_decay <- select_best(network_tuning, metric = "rmse")
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: tune-network-py
#| eval: false
validation_start = date(1995, 1, 1)
decay_grid = {"alpha": [1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000]}

# Estimate until validation_start (-1), choose the weight decay on the years after (0)
validation_fold = np.where(scaled_train["date"] < validation_start, -1, 0)
network_model = MLPRegressor(
    hidden_layer_sizes=(5,),
    activation="logistic",
    solver="lbfgs",
    max_iter=500,  # as in nnet; scikit-learn warns when lbfgs stops here, nnet does not
    random_state=1,
)
network_search = GridSearchCV(
    network_model,
    decay_grid,
    scoring="neg_mean_squared_error",
    cv=PredefinedSplit(validation_fold),
)
network_search.fit(scaled_train.select(features), scaled_train["ret_scaled"])
```
:::

## An ensemble of networks

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: ensemble-network-r
#| cache: true
#| dependson: "tune-network-r"
#| cache.extra: !expr list(rlang::hash(scaled_train), rlang::hash(scaled_panel), ret_sd)
n_networks <- 5

# The average forecast of networks from different random starts
network_forecasts <- map(seq_len(n_networks), \(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  network_fit <- network_workflow |>
    finalize_workflow(best_decay) |>
    fit(scaled_train)
  predict(network_fit, scaled_panel)$.pred * ret_sd
})
network_forecast <- reduce(network_forecasts, `+`) / n_networks
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: ensemble-network-py
#| eval: false
n_networks = 5

# The average forecast of networks from different random starts
network_forecasts = []
for seed in range(1, n_networks + 1):
    network = clone(network_search.best_estimator_).set_params(random_state=seed)
    network.fit(scaled_train.select(features), scaled_train["ret_scaled"])
    network_forecasts.append(network.predict(scaled_panel.select(features)) * ret_sd)
network_forecast = np.mean(network_forecasts, axis=0)
```
:::

- `scaled_train`, `scaled_panel`: predictors standardized, returns divided by their standard deviation `ret_sd`, both with the estimation sample. The forecasts come back in returns: times `ret_sd`
- `manual_rset()` and `PredefinedSplit()` made the one validation split a resample for `tune_grid()` and `GridSearchCV()`; `finalize_workflow()` and `best_estimator_` carry the chosen decay into every network

```{r}
#| label: network-row
#| include: false
network_row <- forecast_row("Neural network", network_forecast)
ols_fit <- lm(reformulate(features, response = "ret"), data = train)
ols_row <- forecast_row("OLS", predict(ols_fit, panel))
```

## The network's forecasts

- One hidden layer of `r hidden_units` logistic neurons. Inputs: the `r length(features)` predictors of lecture 13, standardized with the estimation sample; target: the return in units of its standard deviation $\sigma_r$ in the estimation sample
- **Weight decay** $\lambda$: a ridge penalty on the $K = `r n_parameters`$ weights and constants $\theta_k$ in $\theta$, added to the squared forecast errors of the $T$ months of the estimation sample:

$$
\min_{\theta} \ \sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \Big(\frac{r_{i,t+1}}{\sigma_r} - g(z_{i,t}; \theta)\Big)^2 + \lambda \sum_{k=1}^{K} \theta_k^2
$$

- $\lambda = `r best_decay$penalty`$, chosen on `r year(validation_start)`–`r year(test_start) - 1` from `r min(decay_grid$penalty)` to `r comma(max(decay_grid$penalty))`; `r n_networks` networks from different random starts averaged
- Out-of-sample $R^2$ `r percent(network_row$oos_r2, 0.01)` (OLS: `r percent(ols_row$oos_r2, 0.01)`); as a portfolio with the forecasts as expected returns (lecture 13): Sharpe ratio `r number(network_row$test, 0.01)` in the test sample
- nnet and scikit-learn use the same penalty scale, but scikit-learn leaves the constants unpenalized and starts from other random weights, so their networks differ a little

# Learning the SDF

## SDF weights that depend on the state

::: {.box}
Lecture 11: the same weights $b_i$ in every month, $M_{t+1} = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{N} b_i F_{i,t+1}$, with $b$ proportional to $\Sigma^{-1}\mu$. Now each anomaly's weight depends on what we know at $t$:

$$
M_{t+1} = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{N} \omega(I_t, z_{i,t})\, F_{i,t+1}
$$
:::

- $I_t$: the **macro state**, the same for all anomalies; $z_{i,t}$: the **features** of anomaly $i$, such as its last return and its momentum. $\omega$ is a feed-forward network, the same for all $N$ anomalies

::: {.fragment}
$$
E_t\big[M_{t+1} F_{i,t+1}\big] = 0 \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad E\big[M_{t+1} F_{i,t+1}\, g(I_t, z_{i,t})\big] = 0 \ \text{ for all functions } g
$$

- The conditional moments hold for every **instrument** $g$: every managed portfolio $F_{i,t+1}\, g(I_t, z_{i,t})$ must be priced, too
- The network $\omega$ minimizes the squared pricing errors $E\big[M_{t+1} F_{i,t+1}\, g(I_t, z_{i,t})\big]^2$ for a set of instruments $g$. Which ones? Next slide
:::

## The adversary

- Infinitely many instruments $g$: which ones should the SDF price? Chen, Pelger & Zhu (2024): let a **second network** choose them, a feed-forward network with the same inputs as $\omega$
- The adversary $g$ picks the managed portfolios with the **largest pricing errors**; the SDF network $\omega$ then learns to price them. Chen, Pelger & Zhu call this game a generative adversarial network (GAN):

$$
\min_{\omega} \ \max_{g} \ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \bigg\| E\bigg[\Big(1 - \sum_{j=1}^{N} \omega(I_t, z_{j,t})\, F_{j,t+1}\Big) F_{i,t+1}\, g(I_t, z_{i,t})\bigg] \bigg\|^2
$$

- $g$ has several outputs, one instrument each; $\|\cdot\|^2$ adds up their squared pricing errors
- Their result on US stocks: an SDF with an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio far above linear factor models. Inputs: 46 firm characteristics and the **macro state**, a few variables that a recurrent network (LSTM) extracts from 178 macroeconomic time series

## Chen–Pelger–Zhu light on the zoo

```{r}
#| label: cpz-results
#| include: false
# The search on UCloud: every setting with ensembles of nine networks
ensemble_size <- 9
cpz_results <- "lecture-slides/factor-zoo/results"
cpz_runs <- read_csv(
  file.path(cpz_results, "cpz_light_runs.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  filter(seeds == ensemble_size) |>
  mutate(
    model = if_else(
      str_detect(model, "Chen"),
      "Chen–Pelger–Zhu light",
      "Feed-forward SDF"
    )
  )
n_settings <- n_distinct(
  cpz_runs$hidden,
  cpz_runs$dropout,
  cpz_runs$weight_decay,
  cpz_runs$pcs,
  cpz_runs$no_macro
)
cpz_chosen <- cpz_runs |> slice_max(sr_valid, n = 1, by = model)
cpz_light <- cpz_chosen |> filter(model == "Chen–Pelger–Zhu light")
feed_forward <- cpz_chosen |> filter(model == "Feed-forward SDF")
cpz_correlation <- cpz_runs |>
  summarize(correlation = cor(sr_valid, sr_test), .by = model) |>
  deframe()

# The networks' returns start once every input has a year of history
cpz_start <- list.files(
  cpz_results,
  paste0("^cpz_light_sdf_returns_seeds-", ensemble_size),
  full.names = TRUE
)[1] |>
  read_parquet() |>
  pull(date) |>
  min()
validation_years <- paste0(year(validation_start), "–", year(test_start) - 1)
```

- **Two networks** as in Chen, Pelger & Zhu, each with two hidden layers (ReLU activation and dropout): the SDF network $\omega$, and the adversary $g$ with `r cpz_light$instruments` instruments per anomaly
- **Inputs of each anomaly:** last month's return, factor momentum, its historical mean, its loadings on the first `r max(cpz_runs$pcs)` principal components; optionally the macro state, here the `r length(macro_names)` macro predictors of lecture 13 instead of an LSTM`r if (cpz_light$no_macro) " (the chosen setting leaves it out)"`
- **Steps:** the SDF network first prices the unconditional moments ($g = 1$); then, `r cpz_light$rounds` times, the adversary picks the instruments with the largest pricing errors and the SDF network learns to price them
- **Training** `r year(cpz_start)`–`r year(validation_start) - 1`, **validation** `r validation_years` (early stopping and the choice of the setting), test from `r year(test_start)`. PyTorch only: `lecture-slides/factor-zoo/cpz_light.py`, `r n_settings` settings × `r ensemble_size` networks, 2 h 14 min on 64 UCloud cores

## What the networks earn

```{r}
#| label: plot-cpz
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.3
ggplot(cpz_runs, aes(x = sr_valid, y = sr_test, color = model)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = ridge_sharpe[["test"]],
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = grey
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = min(cpz_runs$sr_valid),
    y = ridge_sharpe[["test"]],
    label = "Ridge SDF",
    hjust = 0,
    vjust = -0.5,
    color = grey
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = cpz_chosen, size = 5, shape = 21, stroke = 1.3, fill = NA) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Chen–Pelger–Zhu light" = ku_red, "Feed-forward SDF" = "#b3b3b3")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("Sharpe ratio, validation ", validation_years, " (annualized)"),
    y = paste0("Sharpe ratio, test ", test_years, "\n(annualized)"),
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

- Each dot is one of the `r n_settings` settings; circles: the setting chosen on the validation sample. The adversary helps: `r number(cpz_light$sr_test, 0.01)` against `r number(feed_forward$sr_test, 0.01)` without it
- For Chen–Pelger–Zhu light, the validation Sharpe ratio predicts the test Sharpe ratio (correlation `r number(cpz_correlation[["Chen–Pelger–Zhu light"]], 0.01)`). But no setting reaches the ridge SDF

## Flexibility against economic structure

- **Nagel (2021):** returns are noisy and samples are short; machine learning in asset pricing works best with economic restrictions, such as a prior that rules out implausibly high Sharpe ratios
- **Our out-of-sample comparison:** `r ncol(returns)` anomalies, `r year(test_start) - year(sample_start)` years of estimation data. The ridge SDF has one tuning parameter and an economic prior; the networks have thousands of parameters and only the data
- Gu, Kelly & Xiu and Chen, Pelger & Zhu use tens of thousands of stocks and decades of data: there, flexibility pays

::: {.highlight}
The more data, the more flexibility can pay; with little data, economic structure wins
:::

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| echo: false
# Every row of lectures 10 to 14
bind_rows(
  sdf_rows,
  tibble(
    Portfolio = paste(
      "Forecasts:",
      c(
        "OLS",
        paste("tree of depth", tree_depth),
        "random forest",
        "neural network"
      )
    ),
    Inputs = paste(
      c(
        length(features),
        length(attr(tree$terms, "term.labels")),
        length(features),
        length(features)
      ),
      "predictors"
    ),
    estimation = c(
      ols_row$estimation,
      tree_row$estimation,
      forest_row$estimation,
      network_row$estimation
    ),
    test = c(ols_row$test, tree_row$test, forest_row$test, network_row$test)
  ),
  tibble(
    Portfolio = c("Feed-forward SDF", "Chen–Pelger–Zhu light"),
    Inputs = "Features of each anomaly",
    estimation = c(feed_forward$sr_estimation, cpz_light$sr_estimation),
    test = c(feed_forward$sr_test, cpz_light$sr_test)
  )
) |>
  mutate(across(c(estimation, test), \(x) number(x, 0.01))) |>
  rename(
    `Sharpe ratio, estimation` = estimation,
    !!paste("Sharpe ratio", test_years) := test
  )
```

- Penalties and numbers of factors chosen by cross-validation, network settings on `r validation_years`. The forecasts' estimation sample starts in `r format(min(panel$date), "%B %Y")`, after a year of history
- **Lecture 15:** what all these portfolios trade, and what remains after costs
